751.quote_or_event: “Nanak seeks the company of the lowest of the low class, the very lowest of the low. Why should he try to compete with the great?”
751.explanation: Guru Nanak deliberately turns away from the esteem the world gives to the wealthy and powerful, and places himself among those whom society counts as nothing.
751.tie_back: The Kural observes that only wealth turns people of no account into people who count; Guru Nanak answers that observation by choosing the company of those who count for nothing in the world's eyes.
751.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
751._accuracy_note: A counterpoint rather than a parallel: Gurbani recognises the same social fact but rejects wealth as the measure of worth, so the match is thematic contrast only.

752.quote_or_event: “No one respects the poor man. He may make thousands of efforts, but no one pays any attention to him. When the poor man goes to the rich man, and sits right in front of him, the rich man turns his back on him. But when the rich man goes to the poor man, the poor man welcomes him with respect.”
752.explanation: Bhagat Kabir describes how the world slights the poor and honours the rich, then concludes that the two are brothers and that the truly poor one is he who lacks the Name in his heart.
752.tie_back: The Kural says everyone scorns those who have nothing and honours the rich; Kabir paints the very same scene, almost line for line.
752.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1159, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
752._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one as description of the world's behaviour; Kabir's conclusion, that real poverty is lacking the Name, goes beyond the Kural's point about the value of wealth.

753.quote_or_event: “The One Name is my lamp; I have put the oil of suffering into it.”
753.explanation: Guru Nanak names the divine Name as the lamp that lights his way, burning away suffering as its oil.
753.tie_back: The Kural calls wealth an unfailing lamp that cuts through darkness wherever its owner goes; Guru Nanak's unfailing lamp is the Name, which Gurbani treats as the true wealth.
753.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 358, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
753._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the shared image is the lamp that dispels darkness, but the Kural's lamp is material wealth overcoming enmity abroad, while Guru Nanak's is spiritual and dispels suffering and death.

754.quote_or_event: “To take what rightfully belongs to another, is like a Muslim eating pork, or a Hindu eating beef.”
754.explanation: In a salok of Maajh ki Vaar, Guru Nanak declares that wealth taken from another's rightful share is as forbidden as the most abhorrent food in each faith.
754.tie_back: The Kural says wealth gained by right means and without wrongdoing gives birth to virtue and happiness; Guru Nanak draws the boundary from the other side, condemning wealth taken unjustly as utterly unclean.
754.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Raag Maajh (Maajh ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
754._accuracy_note: Strong on the condition 'without evil', but the salok states only the prohibition and does not speak of the virtue and happiness that honest wealth produces.

755.quote_or_event: “For the sake of this wealth, so many were ruined; because of this wealth, so many have been disgraced. It was not gathered without sin, and it does not go along with the dead.”
755.explanation: Reflecting on the fall of the Lodi nobility before Babur, Guru Nanak says that their hoarded wealth brought ruin and disgrace, because it had been gathered through wrongdoing.
755.tie_back: The Kural tells us to let wealth gained without compassion and love roll away rather than embrace it; Guru Nanak shows what such wealth does to those who cling to it.
755.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa (Ashtapadi, Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
755._accuracy_note: A strong fit on rejecting wealth acquired without righteousness; the Kural frames the test as compassion and love, while Guru Nanak frames it as sin and its consequences.

756.quote_or_event: Under Guru Arjan a cadre of local leaders called masands looked after the Sikh sangats in distant places and collected from the disciples dasvandh, one-tenth of their income, which they were enjoined to give for communal sharing; by encouraging agriculture and trade and introducing this tithe for the common use of the community, a stable economic base was secured. When complaints arose against the masands, Guru Gobind Singh in 1698 told the Sikhs to bring their offerings to him directly.
756.explanation: The early Sikh community had defined, lawful channels of revenue, and when collectors abused them the Guru reformed the system.
756.tie_back: The Kural lists the lawful sources of a ruler's treasury; the Sikh Gurus likewise built a common treasury on a clearly defined, voluntary tithe and removed the intermediaries who misused it.
756.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entries Arjan Dev, Guru and Gobind Singh, Guru
756._accuracy_note: Next-best: both concern legitimate revenue, but dasvandh is a voluntary religious offering for communal sharing, not a king's escheats, customs and war tribute, which the Kural lists; the 1698 reform is from the Gobind Singh entry.

757.quote_or_event: When Guru Nanak left his post as storekeeper to the Nawab of Sultanpur, complaints were made of his extravagance; but on investigation the storehouse was found full and his accounts correct, and money was even found due to him from the State, which the Guru refused, asking the Nawab to spend it in relieving the wants of the poor.
757.explanation: Macauliffe, following the Janamsakhi tradition, tells how Nanak's honestly kept wealth, far from being lost, became a means of care for the poor.
757.tie_back: The Kural pictures compassion as a child nursed by the rich foster-mother called wealth; in this story honestly earned wealth is turned at once into the nourishment of compassion.
757.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. 1 (1909), Life of Guru Nanak, pp. 42-43
757._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of wealth serving compassion, but it is hagiography drawn from the Janamsakhi tradition, and it lacks the Kural's genealogy of love begetting compassion.

758.quote_or_event: “Reliance on mortals is in vain - know this well.”
758.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan teaches that leaning on other people for support is futile, and that the one Giver is God.
758.tie_back: The Kural says one who undertakes a task with his own means in hand can watch the struggle safely, free of dependence on others; Guru Arjan likewise warns against depending on other people.
758.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 281, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani Sahib), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
758._accuracy_note: Next-best only: both value independence from others, but the Kural's security lies in one's own funds, while Guru Arjan's lies in God alone; no Gurbani passage praises self-financing as such.

759.quote_or_event: “From the Guru, I have obtained the supremely powerful sword of spiritual wisdom.”
759.explanation: Guru Ram Das names the Guru's wisdom as the sharpest of swords, the weapon with which the enemies within, the passions and ego, are cut down.
759.tie_back: The Kural says there is no steel sharper than wealth for cutting down a foe's pride; Gurbani names a different sharpest blade, the Guru's wisdom, which cuts down one's own pride.
759.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1087, Raag Maaroo, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
759._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the shared image is the sharpest sword against pride, but the Kural recommends accumulating wealth to humble enemies, which Gurbani does not teach; Sikhism turns the weapon against haumai within.

760.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
760.explanation: In a salok of Saarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak sums up the Sikh householder ideal: earn honestly by one's own labour and share part of it with others.
760.tie_back: The Kural says that for those who have gathered honest wealth, virtue and happiness follow easily; Guru Nanak says that the one who earns honestly and shares has found the true path of life.
760.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
760._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on honest earning as the basis of a complete life; Gurbani adds the duty of sharing (vand chhakna) and frames the goal as the spiritual path rather than the Kural's aims of virtue and pleasure.
